newsitem.title: FRANCE: RENAULT WOES SIGNAL HAZARDS AHEAD.
newsitem.headline: RENAULT WOES SIGNAL HAZARDS AHEAD.

text.p: French carmaker Renault's plan to axe 6,000 jobs has caused public outrage, but more cuts are on the way as Europe's auto industry prepares for all-out competition at the turn of the century.
Voluntary quotas limiting Japanese exports to Europe expire in the year 2000, and low-cost Korean producers have drafted ambitious plans to carve out pieces of the European market.
"This is the biggest bloc in the world -- 13 million units -- and the last market where the non-European players have a chance of getting in," said Goldman Sachs analyst Keith Hayes.

France's two car companies Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen look particularly vulnerable. They are small by global standards and much more dependent on the European market than rivals Volkswagen and Fiat .
The French sell only 15 percent of their cars outside Europe, having retreated from tough markets such as the United States and made a late start in Asia and Latin America.

Their home market is crumbling after the end of state buying incentives -- car sales were down 29 percent in the first two months of 1997 -- and France has become the main battleground of a fierce price war being waged across Europe.

Analysts say the French also lag their rivals in industrial efficiency. "They run quite a few plants considering how small they are, with nine plants each," said analyst John Lawson at Salomon Brothers. "It's an expensive structure to support."

Last month Renault conceded that it was in serious trouble and said it would close a high-cost plant at Vilvoorde in Belgium which employs 3,100 people. It will also accelerate its job-reduction programme in France, cutting 2,764 jobs in 1997 after 1,640 last year from a total work force of nearly 141,000.
EURO-RESTRUCTURING PROMPTS EURO-PROTESTS
French, Belgian, and European Union leaders blasted Renault for the abrupt manner in which it broke the news.
The Spanish government suspended subsidies to modernise Renault's plant in Valladolid.
Unions staged cross-border strikes and protests to insist on common social standards in an economically integrating Europe.
President Jacques Chirac disapproved of the way the closure was handled but added plant closures "are, alas, part of life".
Other politicians, anxious to bring down France's record 12.7 percent jobless rate before parliamentary elections next March, called for chairman Louis Schweitzer's resignation.
Renault's European staff representatives may launch legal action over the closure. The French staff committee voted on Thursday to delay its examination of the job-cutting plan.
At the other end of the spectrum, financial analysts say Renault's actions may not be tough enough to end its losses, estimated at between five and six billion francs ($1 billion) for 1996.

Despite cost-cutting measures, expected to save around two billion francs, a consensus forecast compiled by consultants Jacques Chahine Finance shows the market does not expect Renault to attain its objective of breaking even this year.
Analysts are watching to see if Schweitzer can push through the measures on the car operations and turn his attention to the truck business, which also plunged into the red last year.
The embattled chairman has spent the past two weeks telling critics, including Renault's biggest shareholder, the government, which owns 46 percent, that he had no alternative.

He told a parliamentary panel that the entire industry was taking painful measures, citing 1,900 layoffs by Volkswagen at a plant near Vilvoorde two years ago as part of a restructuring. This year, Ford Motor Co plans to cut 980 jobs at its Halewood plant in Britain, sparking a new wave of car industry layoffs.
TOO MUCH CAPACITY, TOO FEW BUYERS
"The car industry as a whole will register a drop in staff levels. Unfortunately, from here to the year 2000, I expect further job reductions at Renault," Schweitzer said.
One reason is that sales growth in Europe is stagnating. "We don't expect to recover the sales levels of 1989-1992 until the year 2000, and we're still below 1989 levels," he said.
The Peugeot group expects European sales to grow just 0.5 percent this year from 12.8 million units in 1996. In France, sales are expected to fall 10 percent this year.
But production capacity in Europe has surged to between 16 and 18 million units. The Economist Intelligence Unit estimates it will grow eight times faster than demand to the year 2000.

The problem is most acute when capacity is poorly organised. Renault is struggling to adjust capacity to assemble more Megane Scenic cars at its Douai plant to fill a backlog of orders, but has too much capacity for less popular models.
"The lesson is that everyone has to adjust and be fast on their feet," Lawson said.
ASIANS, EAST EUROPEANS AROUND THE CORNER

Analysts say European carmakers need to become more flexible and cost-efficient -- while producing models at a faster pace -- before barriers holding back their Asian rivals come down. Japan's giant Toyota Motor Corp said on Monday that it was considering additional investment in Europe in response to a Financial Times report that it could build a second European plant in France.
In addition to the much-feared Japanese and Koreans, producers in western Europe face competition from low-cost plants appearing in central and eastern Europe.
"I'm worried when I see that in the Czech Republic, salaries are 15 percent of French levels, and factories run by Volkswagen are perfectly efficient," Schweitzer said.
He said a streamlining of Renault car assembly operations after the closure of Vilvoorde would give the company "the best industrial performance that can be found in Europe".
Although the Peugeot group has fared better, it is expected to report a second consecutive fall in profits for 1996. Its profit margin has been declining for years.
Chairman Jacques Calvet said in December the group might have to lay off workers if the government did not agree to help finance more early retirements.

The government rejected a joint request by the two companies to help finance 40,000 early retirements at a cost of 42 billion francs. Calvet, himself due to retire in September, has been silent but the stock has risen on restructuring expectations.
"Investors expect them to announce some restructuring move after Renault's actions," a trader said last Friday.
The industry's troubles have revived the question of whether France can sustain two carmakers, particularly since Renault's proposed linkup with Sweden's Volvo collapsed in 1994.
Analysts eyeing possible partners for Renault and Peugeot say Fiat and Mercedes both offer potential synergies.
Both French companies rule out merging with each other and have strong enough balance sheets to survive many lean years.

"If the two groups were brought together...the French industry would be the first casualty because we'd see sales volumes and market share collapse," Schweitzer said, although he forecast greater collaboration on engines and other components.
"A merger with another carmaker? Never, never, never and definitely not with another French carmaker," Calvet said at this month's Geneva car show. ($ = 5.72 French Francs)
